questions.question: What is the difference between a unit test and an integration test in Spring Boot?
questions.title: Unit vs Integration Test
questions.direct_answer: A unit test checks a single class in isolation using mocks, while an integration test boots (part of) the Spring context and tests real wiring between components.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the testing pyramid and knows when each test type is appropriate
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying unit tests use @SpringBootTest, or conflating the two types
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the testing pyramid and trade-offs: unit tests are faster and more focused; integration tests give higher confidence but are slower

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A unit test focuses on a single class or method in complete isolation. You replace all dependencies — like services or repositories — with mocks so the test only ever exercises the logic inside that one class. There's no Spring context loaded at all, which makes unit tests extremely fast. You typically use JUnit 5 with Mockito for this.

An integration test, on the other hand, checks that multiple components work correctly together. In Spring Boot, this usually means loading some or all of the application context so that real beans are wired up. When you annotate a test class with @SpringBootTest, Spring boots up the full context, and you can test real controller-to-service-to-repository flows.

The key trade-off is speed versus confidence. Unit tests run in milliseconds and pinpoint exactly what broke, but they can miss problems that only appear when real components interact. Integration tests give you higher confidence in end-to-end behavior, but they take significantly longer because of the context startup overhead.

In practice, most teams follow the testing pyramid: many unit tests at the base, a moderate number of integration tests in the middle, and very few end-to-end tests at the top. For a Spring Boot project, a typical rule of thumb is: test your business logic with unit tests, test your REST layer with @WebMvcTest, and test your data layer with @DataJpaTest. Reserve @SpringBootTest for full end-to-end integration scenarios.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Unit test: single class, all dependencies mocked, no Spring context, very fast
Integration test: multiple components wired together, Spring context loaded, slower
@SpringBootTest loads full context — use it for integration tests, not unit tests
Testing pyramid: many unit tests, fewer integration tests, fewest e2e tests

questions.question: Why are unit tests faster than integration tests in a Spring Boot application?
questions.title: Why Unit Tests Are Faster
questions.direct_answer: Unit tests have no Spring context startup cost and no I/O — they run pure Java logic against in-memory mocks in milliseconds.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of what actually makes tests slow — context startup, I/O, network
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying unit tests are faster simply because they have less code
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Spring context startup can take several seconds, which multiplies across a test suite

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The main reason unit tests are so much faster is that they don't start a Spring application context. When Spring Boot launches a context, it has to scan all your configuration classes, create bean definitions, wire up dependencies, and potentially connect to a database or message broker. That process alone can take 2 to 10 seconds depending on the project size.

Unit tests skip all of that entirely. They call your Java class directly, and anywhere a dependency is needed they use a Mockito mock — which is just a Java proxy object created in microseconds. There's no I/O, no network, no file system access.

This matters a lot at scale. If you have 500 unit tests that each take 10 milliseconds, your full suite runs in 5 seconds. If you have 500 integration tests that each start a Spring context, even with context caching each new context variant adds seconds to your build. CI pipelines become painfully slow, which discourages developers from running tests frequently.

This is why the testing pyramid recommends keeping the bulk of your tests as unit tests — you get fast feedback loops during development, and you only pay the context startup cost for the scenarios where real integration is being tested.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Spring context startup is the main cost of integration tests — can take 2-10 seconds
Unit tests use Mockito mocks which are in-memory Java objects, no I/O
Spring caches contexts between tests, but each unique context configuration still adds overhead
Fast unit tests enable short feedback loops during development

questions.question: In a Spring Boot project, what does a typical unit test look like compared to an integration test?
questions.title: Unit vs Integration Test Structure
questions.direct_answer: A unit test uses @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) with @Mock for dependencies; an integration test uses @SpringBootTest to load the context.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can write or recognize both test types and knows the annotation difference
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @SpringBootTest on a service unit test, wasting context startup time
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the code structure from memory and explain why each annotation is chosen

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A unit test in Spring Boot typically looks like this: you annotate the class with @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class), declare your dependencies with @Mock, and inject them into your class under test with @InjectMocks. There's no Spring involved at all — Mockito handles the wiring. Your test method then stubs the mocks with when().thenReturn() and asserts on the result.

For example, testing an OrderService that depends on an OrderRepository: you'd create a mock OrderRepository, inject it into the OrderService, stub the repository's findById to return a sample order, and then assert that the service returns the expected result. The whole test runs in milliseconds.

An integration test looks quite different. You annotate the class with @SpringBootTest, which tells Spring Boot to start the full application context. You can then @Autowire real beans — the actual OrderService with the actual OrderRepository connected to a real (or in-memory H2) database. You might use @Transactional to roll back after each test. The test is slower but proves that all the real wiring works correctly.

The structural rule of thumb: if you only need to test logic, use @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class). If you need to test how beans interact, use a Spring-based annotation like @SpringBootTest, @WebMvcTest, or @DataJpaTest.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Unit test: @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) + @Mock + @InjectMocks — no Spring
Integration test: @SpringBootTest — loads full application context
@Transactional on integration tests rolls back DB changes after each test
Choosing the right annotation avoids unnecessary context startup overhead

questions.question: What is the testing pyramid and how does it apply to Spring Boot applications?
questions.title: Testing Pyramid in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: The testing pyramid recommends many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests in the middle, and very few slow end-to-end tests at the top.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate has a structured view of testing strategy, not just individual annotations
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing integration tests for everything or ignoring unit tests entirely
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Map each Spring testing annotation to its pyramid layer

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The testing pyramid is a concept introduced by Mike Cohn that describes the ideal distribution of tests in a software project. At the base of the pyramid you have unit tests — the most numerous, the cheapest to write, and the fastest to run. In the middle are integration tests, fewer in number but testing real interactions between components. At the top are end-to-end tests, fewest of all because they're slow, brittle, and expensive to maintain.

In a Spring Boot application, this maps quite cleanly to the available annotations. Unit tests — the pyramid base — use plain JUnit 5 with Mockito and no Spring at all. Service logic, utility classes, validators: all of these belong in unit tests.

The middle layer uses Spring's test slices: @WebMvcTest for controller tests with a minimal web context, @DataJpaTest for repository tests with only the JPA layer loaded. These are integration tests, but they're narrow integration tests — they don't load your full application.

At the top, @SpringBootTest with a real server (or TestRestTemplate) represents your full integration and end-to-end tests. These verify that all layers work together, but you keep these few in number.

A healthy Spring Boot project might have 200 unit tests, 40 slice tests, and 10 full @SpringBootTest tests. This keeps the CI pipeline fast while still giving you high confidence.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Base: many unit tests — JUnit + Mockito, no Spring context
Middle: slice tests — @WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest (partial context, faster)
Top: few full integration tests — @SpringBootTest (whole context)
Goal: fast feedback + high confidence at minimal cost

questions.question: Should you test your Spring service layer with unit tests or integration tests? Why?
questions.title: Testing the Service Layer
questions.direct_answer: Test service layer business logic with unit tests using mocked repositories — integration tests are not needed unless you're verifying real database transactions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical judgment about which test type belongs at which layer
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @SpringBootTest for every service test, making the suite very slow
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the clear separation: service = unit test (mock the repo), controller = slice test, repo = @DataJpaTest

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
For the service layer, unit tests are almost always the right choice. The service layer contains your business logic — validation rules, calculations, orchestration between multiple repositories. None of that logic actually depends on Spring or a real database to be verified. You can mock the repository with Mockito, call the service method, and assert on the result.

This approach keeps your service tests extremely fast and focused. If a service test fails, you know the issue is in the service logic itself, not in the database query or the HTTP layer.

You'd only write an integration test for a service if you specifically need to verify transactional behavior — for example, testing that a rollback happens correctly when an exception is thrown mid-operation, or testing that two service methods that share a transaction behave correctly together. Those scenarios require a real Spring context with a real database (or an in-memory H2), so they justify the overhead.

The general layered approach is: service logic → unit test with @Mock repository, controller/HTTP layer → @WebMvcTest with @MockBean service, repository/database queries → @DataJpaTest, full end-to-end → @SpringBootTest. Following this keeps your test suite fast, maintainable, and well-organized.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Service business logic should be unit tested with Mockito mocks — no Spring needed
Only use integration tests for services when testing real transactional behavior
Mock the repository layer so service tests are isolated and fast
Each layer has its natural test type: controller=@WebMvcTest, repo=@DataJpaTest

questions.question: What happens when you annotate a test with @SpringBootTest?
questions.title: What @SpringBootTest Does
questions.direct_answer: @SpringBootTest triggers Spring Boot's full application context startup, loading all beans and auto-configurations as if the application were running normally.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic understanding of what @SpringBootTest actually does under the hood
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that it starts a full context, including database connections and configuration loading
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention webEnvironment parameter options (MOCK, RANDOM_PORT, DEFINED_PORT) and context caching

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
When you annotate a test class with @SpringBootTest, Spring Boot performs its full context initialization — the same startup process that happens when you run the application normally. It finds your main @SpringBootApplication class, scans for all @Component, @Service, @Repository, and @Controller beans, applies all auto-configurations, and loads your application.properties or application.yml. If you have a database configured, it will try to connect to it.

@SpringBootTest also accepts a webEnvironment parameter that controls how the web server is set up. MOCK (the default) creates a mock servlet environment without starting a real HTTP server — this is used with MockMvc. RANDOM_PORT starts a real embedded Tomcat on a random port, which is needed for TestRestTemplate or WebTestClient tests. DEFINED_PORT uses the port in your config.

One important performance optimization: Spring Boot caches the application context between test classes. If multiple test classes use the exact same context configuration, they share one context rather than each starting their own. This is why you should avoid @DirtiesContext unless necessary — it forces the context to be rebuilt, discarding the cache.

The bottom line is: @SpringBootTest is your heaviest test tool and gives the most realistic environment. Use it when you need the full stack, and prefer slices when you only need one layer.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Loads full application context — all beans, auto-configurations, properties
webEnvironment=MOCK (default): mock servlet, use with MockMvc
webEnvironment=RANDOM_PORT: real server, use with TestRestTemplate
Spring caches context between tests — avoid @DirtiesContext to keep it fast

questions.question: Can a Spring Boot test be both a unit test and use Spring annotations at the same time?
questions.title: Mixing Unit and Spring Annotations
questions.direct_answer: No — a true unit test doesn't load a Spring context; mixing Spring annotations defeats the purpose and adds overhead without benefit.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate has clear conceptual boundaries between test types
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding @SpringBootTest to tests that only test a service method, treating all tests as integration tests
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) is the correct choice for unit tests and doesn't involve Spring at all

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Technically you could add @SpringBootTest to a test that only tests one class, but it would be a mistake. The moment you add @SpringBootTest, Spring starts the full application context, which takes several seconds — and you've gained nothing, because your test is still only exercising a single class.

A true unit test is defined by its isolation: it tests one class, all dependencies are mocked, and there's no external system involved. The correct annotation for a unit test in Spring Boot is @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class), which is a JUnit 5 extension that activates Mockito's annotation processing. It has absolutely nothing to do with Spring.

The confusion often comes from seeing both @ExtendWith(SpringExtension.class) and @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) in codebases. SpringExtension integrates Spring's context with JUnit 5 and is used internally by @SpringBootTest and the slice annotations. MockitoExtension is purely for Mockito and doesn't touch Spring at all.

The practical rule: if your test class needs Spring beans, use a Spring annotation (@SpringBootTest, @WebMvcTest, etc.). If it only needs mocks of plain Java objects, use @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) and keep it a true unit test.

Adding @SpringBootTest to a unit test wastes time starting an unneeded context
SpringExtension is used by Spring-based test annotations internally
Clear boundary: need Spring beans = use Spring annotation; otherwise use Mockito only
